descs.t: Benjamin Netanyahu pushed for a strike on Iran before Israel's election on Tuesday, but President Trump refused, CNN reports, and Israeli outlets say IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir objected to the plan. CNN also reports Israel has suspended plans for more strikes on Iran in the immediate term. We walk through what is reported and what happens next.

Netanyahu says Israel has fresh intelligence that Iran will launch attacks to disrupt Tuesday's election, while reports say his army chief resisted a strike order and Trump said no. At the same time Trump issued a second endorsement of Netanyahu. We look at what this clash means for Israel's election and for pressure on the Iranian regime.

Netanyahu warns that Iran wants to disrupt Israel's election, and the fight over whether to strike the regime first has reached the top of Israel's army and President Trump. The Times of Israel and Haaretz carry the reports. We break down who said no, why, and what it means for the regime in Tehran.

intro.plain: Big news out of Israel. CNN says Netanyahu pushed for a strike on Iran before Tuesday's election and Trump refused. Israeli reports say the army chief, Eyal Zamir, objected too, and Israel has put further strikes on hold for now. Let's go through what is actually reported and what it means. Chat, should Israel have struck before the vote?
intro.mid: Netanyahu says Iran is planning attacks to disrupt Israel's election on Tuesday. Reports say he wanted to strike first, his army chief pushed back, and Trump said no, while also endorsing him a second time. Let's work out what this means for the election and for the regime. Chat, who do you think made the right call here?
intro.bold: Netanyahu says the regime in Tehran wants to disrupt Israel's election, and he wanted to hit it first. Reports say his army chief resisted and Trump said not now. So the regime gets a pause. Let's look at whether that pause helps anyone but Tehran. Chat, is holding back right now a mistake?

hook.plain: Netanyahu wanted to strike Iran before Tuesday's election. Trump refused, CNN says, and Israel's army chief objected. Here is what happened and what comes next.
hook.mid: Days before Israel votes, Netanyahu, his army chief and Trump split over a strike on Iran. Here is what that clash means for the election and for the regime.
hook.bold: Netanyahu says Iran wants to disrupt Israel's election. He wanted to hit the regime first, and he was told no. Here is who stopped it, and what it costs.

Brazil's Election Result and the Bid to Overturn It
Bolsonaro Ordered to Hand Over Passport a Day After Losing
Did a 2 Hour Voting Extension Decide Brazil's Election?
Lula's Fourth Term and the Fight Over Brazil's Courts

descs.t: Lula da Silva has won a fourth term as Brazil's president, beating Flávio Bolsonaro in the runoff with 51.76% of the vote at 99.8% counted, according to reports. Bolsonaro refuses to concede and says he will ask the courts to annul the result. We walk through the count, the comeback and what Bolsonaro is now asking for.

Brazil's runoff is over on paper, but Flávio Bolsonaro says he cannot recognise Lula's win and blames a late court decision on voting hours. Reports say he was ordered to surrender his passport a day later, and Brazil's currency reportedly fell sharply. We look at the court rulings, the annulment bid and what a fourth Lula term means for Brazil.

Lula has a fourth term and Brazil is split over how he got it. Bolsonaro's camp says the rules were changed mid vote and wants the result thrown out, while Bolsonaro himself is reportedly ordered to hand over his passport. We go through the claims, what the evidence shows so far, and why the fight over Brazil's courts matters far beyond Brazil.

intro.plain: Brazil has a result. Lula da Silva beat Flávio Bolsonaro in the runoff and wins a fourth term, with reports putting him at 51.76% with almost every vote counted. Bolsonaro is refusing to concede and says he will ask the courts to annul it. So tell me in the chat: is this a fair win, or does Bolsonaro have a case?
intro.mid: Lula has won a fourth term in Brazil, and the fight started the same night. Flávio Bolsonaro says he cannot recognise the result, blames a late court decision on voting hours, and reports say he was then ordered to surrender his passport. That is a lot of court power in one election. Chat, would you trust this result?
intro.bold: Lula wins Brazil again, and his opponent says the rules were changed while people were still voting. Flávio Bolsonaro wants the whole thing annulled, and a day later reports say he was told to hand over his passport. When the courts decide this much, people stop trusting elections. So chat, stolen or sour grapes?

hook.plain: Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in Brazil, and the man he beat refuses to accept it. Here is how the count went and what Flávio Bolsonaro is now asking the courts to do.
hook.mid: A late ruling on voting hours, an annulment bid and a passport order, all in two days. Here is what happened after Brazil's runoff, and why the courts are now the story.
hook.bold: Brazil's loser says the rules changed mid vote, and a day later he is reportedly told to give up his passport. Here is the case on both sides, and what it means for Brazil.

descs.t: A UN Commission of Inquiry report claims Israel's 'genocide' in Gaza has continued after the ceasefire, and accuses Israel of war crimes and crimes against humanity. We set out what the report claims and what it rests on.

The UN's Gaza inquiry has again accused Israel of genocide, this time saying it continued after the ceasefire. Critics point to a similar Amnesty report that relied on 15 airstrike cases, five of which are now said to have killed combatants. We look at the charges, the sources and how much weight they can carry.

Another UN report, another genocide charge against Israel, now even after a ceasefire. We go through what the commission claims, the evidence critics say does not hold up, and why so many people stopped trusting UN bodies on Israel.

intro.plain: A UN Commission of Inquiry has a new report out, and it claims Israel's genocide in Gaza continued even after the ceasefire. It also accuses Israel of war crimes and crimes against humanity. These are claims, so let's look at what they rest on. Chat, do you trust UN reports on Israel?
intro.mid: The UN's Gaza inquiry is back with the word genocide, and now says it continued after the ceasefire. Meanwhile critics say a similar Amnesty report rested on 15 airstrike cases, and five of them hit combatants. So how solid is this one? Chat, what would it take for you to believe a report like this?
intro.bold: The UN has accused Israel of genocide again, and this time even the ceasefire did not stop the verdict. When an Amnesty report on the same war leaned on 15 cases and five turned out to be combatants, you have to ask who is checking. Chat, is the UN investigating Israel or prosecuting it?

hook.plain: A UN inquiry now claims Israel's genocide in Gaza continued after the ceasefire. Here is what the report says, and what it is built on.
hook.mid: A new UN genocide charge, and an older report where five of 15 cases hit combatants. Here is how to weigh what the UN is claiming about Gaza.
hook.bold: The ceasefire came and the UN's verdict on Israel did not change. Here is the charge, the evidence, and the holes critics have already found.

descs.t: The Saudi-led coalition says it has destroyed Houthi missile facilities in Yemen, while the Houthis say they targeted Riyadh airport and a Saudi oil pipeline. We go through the latest strikes on both sides and where the fighting stands.

Saudi Arabia is fighting the Houthis and, according to reports, offering them $1 billion through a deal brokered in Tehran to halt their attacks, while Saudi delegations and allies meet in Iran. We look at the war, the talks and who gains from them.

The Houthis are hitting Saudi troops with drone swarms and claim strikes on Riyadh, while Saudi Arabia reportedly offers them $1 billion to stop. We walk through the strikes, the money and why a deal routed through Tehran should worry everyone who wants the regime's proxies gone.

intro.plain: The war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is heating up. The Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi missile facilities, and the Houthis say they targeted Riyadh airport and a Saudi oil pipeline. Chat, where do you think this goes next?
intro.mid: Saudi Arabia is bombing the Houthis and, according to reports, offering them $1 billion to stop, in a deal brokered through Tehran. At the same time delegations are meeting in Iran. So is this a war or a negotiation? Chat, which one is it?
intro.bold: The Houthis are throwing drone swarms at Saudi troops and claiming strikes on Riyadh, and the reported Saudi answer is $1 billion to make them stop, through Tehran of all places. Paying a proxy to behave never ends well. Chat, does Saudi Arabia pay up or fight this out?

hook.plain: The Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi missile sites, and the Houthis say they hit Riyadh. Here is where this war stands right now.
hook.mid: Bombs on one side, a reported $1 billion offer on the other, and talks in Iran. Here is what Saudi Arabia is really doing about the Houthis.
hook.bold: Drone swarms over Saudi troops, claimed strikes on Riyadh, and a reported billion dollar offer to stop. Here is how the Houthis got this far.

descs.t: Serbia's Student List has won Sunday's snap election, ending the 12-year rule of pro-Russian strongman Vucic, with record turnout and a projected 140 of 250 seats. We go through the result and how the students got here.

A student-led movement has ousted Vucic in Serbia peacefully, and is projected to win about 140 of 250 seats. Supporters gathered at Slavija Square in Belgrade, and Serbia now waits to learn how the new leaders will govern. We look at the win, what it means for Russia's influence and the tests ahead.

No fires, no looting, record turnout: Serbia's students voted a 12-year strongman out of power. We walk through how a peaceful movement beat a pro-Russian regime at the ballot box, and why every opposition facing a dictatorship should be watching.

intro.plain: Big result out of Serbia. The Student List won Sunday's snap election and ended Vucic's 12 years in power, with record turnout and about 140 of 250 seats projected. Supporters packed Slavija Square in Belgrade. Chat, did you see this coming?
intro.mid: A pro-Russian strongman just lost power in Serbia, and he lost it to students. The Student List is projected to take about 140 of 250 seats after a record turnout, and the big question now is whether they can govern. Chat, can a protest movement run a country?
intro.bold: Serbia's students just removed a 12-year strongman, peacefully, at the ballot box. No fires, no looting, record turnout, flags in the streets of Belgrade. That is what people power looks like. Chat, what does Serbia teach every country still living under a regime?

hook.plain: Serbia's Student List has won the snap election and ended Vucic's 12 years in power. Here is the result and how they did it.
hook.mid: A pro-Russian strongman out, about 140 of 250 seats for the students. Here is what Serbia's vote changes, and the hard part that starts now.
hook.bold: No fires, no looting, just a record turnout that ended a strongman's 12 years. Here is how Serbia's students won, and why it matters far beyond Belgrade.

descs.t: French President Macron has promised 'concrete measures' over student demands as protests continue across France and fears grow of unrest at Halloween. Students say they will keep protesting despite the government's concessions. We go through what Macron is offering and what the students want.

Macron says the police were unprepared for the riots, and after visiting the vandalised City Hall of Marseille he blamed social media. Students vow more protests even after concessions. We look at why the unrest keeps going and what Macron's social media blame could lead to.

France's government is giving ground and the riots have not stopped. Macron admits the police were caught unprepared and points at social media, while students promise more. We walk through how the far left mobilised so fast, and what happens when a government rewards the street.

intro.plain: France is still in trouble. Macron has promised concrete measures over the students' demands, but the students say they will keep protesting, and there are fears of unrest at Halloween. Chat, do concessions calm this down or make it worse?
intro.mid: Macron says the French police were unprepared for these riots, and after seeing the vandalised City Hall in Marseille he blamed social media. The students got concessions and still say they are not done. Chat, is social media really the problem here?
intro.bold: Macron gave ground, and French cities still have not calmed down. He admits the police were caught off guard, he blames social media, and the students promise more. When a government rewards the street, the street comes back. Chat, what should Macron do now?

hook.plain: Macron has promised concrete measures, and France's students say they will keep protesting anyway. Here is what is on the table and why it has not worked.
hook.mid: Police caught unprepared, a vandalised City Hall in Marseille, and a president blaming social media. Here is what is really driving France's riots.
hook.bold: The government gave in and the streets did not calm down. Here is how France's riots got ahead of the police, and what Macron does next.
